sections.heading: The Pallavas — architects of the Dravidian temple

blocks.text: The **Pallavas of Kanchipuram (~4th–9th c. CE)** dominated the eastern Deccan-Tamil region and pioneered **South Indian (Dravidian) stone temple architecture**. Their greatest rulers: **Mahendravarman I** (the versatile 'Vichitrachitta' — playwright, musician, initiator of rock-cut temples) and **Narasimhavarman I 'Mamalla'** (defeated the Chalukya Pulakeshin II; founded **Mamallapuram/Mahabalipuram**). They fought the long **Pallava-Chalukya conflict** for Deccan supremacy.

rows: Cave temples (Mandagapattu — 'without brick, timber, metal or mortar')
**Mahabalipuram — the Rathas (monolithic 'Pancha Rathas'), Arjuna's Penance (giant relief)**
The first structural stone temples — the Dravidian vimana emerges

items: **Cultural achievement**: the Pallavas made **Kanchipuram a great centre of learning** (Sanskrit + Tamil; the Ghatika/university; Dandin's Dashakumaracharita; Bharavi), patronised the **Bhakti movement (the Alvars-Nayanars flourished in their era, HCOI-018)**, and their **Dravidian temple template (vimana-mandapa-gopuram)** became the model the Cholas perfected (HCOI-016).

**Society & administration**: Brahmadeya land-grants, sabha-village assemblies (the seed of Chola local self-government), a caste-ordered Brahmanical society with rising temple-centred economy and culture.

**The AP/Deccan relevance**: the Pallavas ruled parts of the **southern Andhra region** (their early history is linked to the Krishna-Guntur area — the early Pallava copper-plates are in Prakrit from the Andhra country); the **Pallava-Chalukya-Pandya triangle** shaped the whole southern Deccan including Andhra's borderlands.
**Craft**: the four-stage architecture table (the heart of any Pallava answer) + the Kanchi-learning-and-Bhakti culture + the Dravidian-template legacy + the Andhra connection.

sections.heading: The Chalukyas — Badami and the Eastern branch

blocks.text: The **Chalukyas of Badami (Vatapi) (~6th–8th c. CE)** were the Deccan's dominant power, founded by **Pulakeshin I**, peaking under **Pulakeshin II (who checked Harsha of Kanauj on the Narmada and fought the Pallavas — the Aihole inscription by Ravikirti records his glory)**. Their lasting gift is **temple architecture** — the experimental cradle where **Nagara (northern), Dravida (southern) and the hybrid Vesara** styles were tried side by side at **Aihole ('cradle of Indian temple architecture'), Badami and Pattadakal (UNESCO)**.

rows: Pulakeshin II; **Aihole (Durga, Lad Khan temples), Badami cave temples, Pattadakal (Virupaksha, Sangameshvara)**; Sanskrit-Kannada patronage
Founded by **Kubja Vishnuvardhana** (Pulakeshin II's brother, ~624 CE); ruled coastal Andhra (Vengi — Krishna-Godavari) for ~500 years; **the cradle of Telugu literature**
**Nannaya** ('Adikavi' — the first Telugu poet), under Eastern-Chalukya **Rajaraja Narendra**, began the **Telugu Mahabharatam (Andhra Mahabharatam)** — the birth of written Telugu literature
Chalukyan temples fused north-south styles; the Eastern Chalukyas built temples in the Andhra deltas (Draksharama, Bhimavaram-area, Bhimeswara)

items: **The architectural laboratory**: Aihole-Badami-Pattadakal were where Indian temple styles were **experimentally synthesised** — the birthplace of the Vesara (Deccan hybrid) style and the proving ground the later Rashtrakutas (Ellora) and Hoysalas built on; a pivotal art-history moment.

**The Telugu-literature birth (the crucial AP point)**: the **Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi** patronised **Nannaya**, who under Rajaraja Narendra (11th c.) began the **Andhra Mahabharatam** — the FOUNDING work of written Telugu literature; Nannaya-Tikkana-Errana are the '**Kavitraya**' (trinity of poets) who translated the Mahabharata, and it starts here — Andhra's literary genesis.

**Political significance**: the Badami Chalukyas checked Harsha (keeping the north-south balance) and fought the Pallavas (the Deccan's defining rivalry); the Eastern Chalukyas gave coastal Andhra ~500 years of continuity and a Telugu cultural identity.
**Craft**: the two-branch structure (Badami + Eastern-Vengi) + the architecture laboratory (Aihole-Pattadakal) + the Telugu-literature birth (Nannaya) — the Eastern Chalukyas are the AP core.

sections.heading: Rashtrakutas and the Kalyani Chalukyas — Deccan zenith

blocks.text: The **Rashtrakutas (~753–982 CE)** — founded by **Dantidurga**, overthrowing the Badami Chalukyas — became the **most powerful pan-Indian empire of their time**, intervening in the north (Kanauj tripartite struggle with the Palas and Pratiharas) and dominating the Deccan. Their crowning glory: the **Kailasa Temple at Ellora (Krishna I)** — the world's **largest monolithic rock-cut structure**, carved top-down from a single hill (UNESCO). The **Kalyani (Western) Chalukyas (~973–1189 CE)** — the **Chalukya revival under Tailapa II**, capital Kalyani — succeeded them, patronising Kannada literature and the Vesara temples, and producing **Vijnaneshwara's Mitakshara** (the great legal treatise on inheritance).

rows: **Kailasa Temple Ellora** (Krishna I); Elephanta caves patronage; **Arab-trade prosperity** (Al-Masudi praised Amoghavarsha as a great king); **Amoghavarsha I** — 'Ashoka of the South', wrote **Kavirajamarga (first Kannada literary work)**; Jain patronage

Chalukya revival (Tailapa II); **Vesara temples** (Lakkundi, Dambal, Itagi — 'the Mahadeva temple'); Kannada poets (Ranna, Pampa-era); **Vijnaneshwara's Mitakshara** (Hindu inheritance law); the **Chola-Chalukya wars**
Both were great **Kannada** patrons; the 'three gems' of Kannada (Pampa, Ponna, Ranna) flourished in this Deccan renaissance

items: **The Deccan as the pivot**: for two centuries the Rashtrakutas made the **Deccan the balancing power of India** — no northern or southern empire could ignore them; they participated in the tripartite Kanauj struggle AND dominated the south, a rare pan-Indian Deccan supremacy.

**The Ellora achievement**: the **Kailasa temple** — carved downward from solid basalt, a full temple complex from one rock — is arguably ancient-medieval India's greatest engineering-artistic feat; Ellora's caves (Hindu-Buddhist-Jain together) embody Rashtrakuta religious catholicity.

**Cultural-legal legacy**: the Kannada literary renaissance (Kavirajamarga, the three gems) and the **Mitakshara** (which governed Hindu inheritance across much of India into modern times) are lasting contributions; the Deccan was a cultural powerhouse, not a periphery.

**AP link**: these were Kannada-Deccan (western) powers, but the **Rashtrakuta-Chalukya-Chola contests directly shaped the Andhra-Telangana borderlands** (Vengi was contested), and the **Kakatiyas (HCOI-020) rose as their successors** in the Telugu country — the AP thread runs through the Deccan power-succession.

sections.heading: The Cholas — the Dravidian imperial zenith

blocks.text: The **Imperial Cholas (~850–1279 CE)** of the Kaveri delta built **South India's greatest empire** — a naval-and-agrarian power that projected across the seas. **Rajaraja I** (conquered the Deccan-Sri Lanka-Maldives; built the **Brihadeeswara/Rajarajeswaram Temple, Thanjavur**) and **Rajendra I** (the **Gangaikonda Chola** — marched to the Ganga; the **naval expedition to Srivijaya/Southeast Asia** — a rare Indian maritime conquest) were the giants. The Cholas perfected the **Dravidian temple** and pioneered **local self-government**.

rows: The **Uttaramerur inscriptions** detail the **ur (general assembly) and sabha (Brahmadeya village assembly)** with elected committees (variyams), qualifications, ballot (kudavolai) — one of history's most sophisticated village democracies
**Brihadeeswara Thanjavur (Rajaraja I) — the great vimana; Gangaikondacholapuram; Airavatesvara Darasuram** — the Chola 'living temples' trio (UNESCO); the temple as economic-social-cultural nucleus
The **Chola bronzes (Nataraja — the cosmic dancer)** — the summit of Indian metal sculpture (lost-wax)
**Naval empire** — Sri Lanka, Maldives, the **Srivijaya expedition (Southeast Asia)**; guild-trade (Ayyavole, Manigramam) with China-SE Asia
Tamil literature (Kamban's Ramayana), Shaivism, Bhakti temple-culture

items: **The village-democracy legacy**: the **Uttaramerur inscriptions** are cited as ancient India's most detailed record of **elected local self-government** — committees, eligibility rules, and a lottery-ballot; a genuine (if elite) participatory tradition that resonates with modern Panchayati Raj — the most examinable Chola point.

**The maritime dimension**: the Cholas were **India's greatest naval power** — the Srivijaya expedition and the control of Indian Ocean trade routes made them a maritime empire, spreading Tamil-Hindu culture to Southeast Asia (the Cholas' rare projection of Indian sea-power).

**Art at its summit**: Chola bronze **Nataraja** and the Brihadeeswara vimana represent the peak of Dravidian temple-and-bronze art; the temple was the hub of land, credit, employment and culture — a total institution.

**AP link**: the Cholas conquered the **Vengi (coastal Andhra)** region and fought the Kalyani Chalukyas and the rising **Kakatiyas** for control of the Andhra country — the Chola-Chalukya-Kakatiya contest over Vengi is the AP thread; Chola influence reached the southern Andhra temples.
